## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes the complete workflow for preparing geological rock
samples and analyzing their major-element oxide composition by
wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (WD-XRF). The procedure covers
sample powdering, flux fusion bead preparation, bead polishing, and
instrument operation on the PANalytical XRF spectrometer using the
SuperQ software with the "Geology Beads" application.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Rock, mineral, and geological samples analyzed as
  lithium tetraborate fusion beads for major-element oxide determination
  (e.g., SiO~2~, Al~2~O~3~, Fe~2~O~3~, CaO, MgO, Na~2~O, K~2~O,
  TiO~2~, P~2~O~5~, MnO).
- **Does not apply to:** Pressed-pellet trace-element analysis, handheld
  (portable) XRF measurements, or non-geological materials.
- **Locations:** Rock preparation lab (powdering and polishing),
  analytical lab / wet lab (weighing, fusion), XRF lab (instrument
  operation).


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                        |

| Lab PI            | Approve methods, ensure training compliance            |
| Lab Technician    | Maintain instrument, assist with troubleshooting       |

Contact the lab technician, Jade Star, or Bob with any questions.


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **High-temperature furnace:** The muffle furnace operates at 1000 °C.
  Crucibles and tiles removed from the furnace are extremely hot. Do not
  touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled. Note the burn marks on
  the existing gloves.
- **Compressed air:** Loud; wear ear protection when blowing out equipment.
- **Rock chipper:** Flying rock fragments are common. Always wear safety
  glasses. Never look into the chipper while it is running.
- **Shatterbox:** The unit vibrates intensely and can travel across the
  floor. Get help repositioning it if needed.
- **Chemical reagents:** Dilithium tetraborate flux is a fine powder; avoid
  inhalation. Ethanol is flammable.
- **X-ray radiation:** The XRF instrument contains an X-ray source.
  Follow all posted radiation safety procedures. Do not open the
  instrument lid while the arm is moving or the flap is up.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses (always, in all labs)
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (especially when handling beads and flux)
- [ ] Ear protection (when using compressed air)
- [ ] Heat-resistant gloves (when loading/unloading the furnace)

### General Lab Rules

Before you start, make sure each sample has a unique number. Label all
containers and keep your workspace clean. Consult the safety manuals
posted in each lab. Do not work in the lab without letting someone know
your plans and estimated time. There are phones and safety showers in all
labs.


## 5. Prerequisites and Required Reading

- SOP-L01: Laboratory Safety
- Furnace operating instructions (posted on the wall above the furnace)
- This SOP in full

::: {.callout-important}
Minimize contamination at every step. Wear gloves, clean equipment
thoroughly between samples, and assume any shared equipment is dirty
unless you just cleaned it. When you are done, leave the lab and
equipment cleaner than you found it.
:::

## 7. Procedure

### 7.1 Step 1: Powdering the Sample

A complete fusion batch is 9 samples. If you plan fusions, turn on the
furnace first (see @sec-first-fusion) since it takes about 1 hour to
reach 1000 °C.

#### Chipping

1. Place the sample in a small, labeled container. If the sample is
   large, chip it to a size suitable for grinding and to provide a
   representative subsample.
2. If the sample is weathered, remove weathered surfaces with a hammer
   or by sawing. Rinse the slab, dry with an ethanol rinse and
   compressed air, and ideally dry overnight in the drying oven to
   remove residual water from sawing. If saw marks are present on the
   analysis surface, remove them by dry-sanding with SiC sandpaper.
3. For very coarse-grained samples, use a splitter to obtain a
   representative split. Ask Jade Star or the technician for guidance.
4. Wearing safety glasses, turn on the small rock chipper (switch on
   the power cord). Drop the sample into the opening, covering it with
   the container or the plastic board. **Do not look into the chipper
   while it is running.**
5. Check the chipper drawer level; empty it when full. Transfer chips to
   a labeled container.
6. Clean the chipper: remove the pin from the left side of the bar
   holding the stationary plate. Slide the bar out to the right. Wipe
   all contact surfaces with an ethanol-dampened Kimwipe (both plates,
   sides, and collecting tray).

#### Grinding

7. Lift the shatterbox lid, unscrew the handle (~8 cranks), and remove
   the tungsten carbide head (it is heavy). Remove the top of the bowl
   and confirm the ring and puck are present and clean. If unsure, run
   a scoop of sand for 15 seconds and discard the powder.
8. Add your chips to the bowl (inside and outside the ring). Add one
   drop of ethanol. If you add too much, leave the top off briefly to
   let it evaporate.
9. Replace the bowl lid, set the head in the shatterbox, tighten the
   handle, and close the shatterbox lid.
10. Set the timer to 2 minutes for a fresh sample (30 seconds for a
    touch-up re-grind). Press the green button.
11. Wait for the shatterbox to finish before opening. If it has traveled
    across the floor, get help to reposition it.
12. Remove the head and place it on a clean sheet of white printer paper
    laid over brown butcher paper. Using the brush (middle drawer under
    the side counter; confirm the metal bristle holder is taped over),
    brush powder from the lid, ring, puck, and bowl onto the paper.
    Keep all parts on the edge of the paper so exterior metal surfaces
    do not contact the sample. Funnel the powder into your labeled
    container using the paper. Use a fresh sheet of paper for every sample.

#### Cleaning the Head

13. If powder is stuck, scrub with a green Brillo pad. If that is
    insufficient, run a scoop of sand for 15 seconds and discard the
    powder.
14. Detail all pieces with compressed air (place the hose in the vise
    and hold pieces in the airflow; scrub with the Brillo pad). **Do
    not let the metal hose tip touch any bowl surface.** Use ear
    protection.
15. Finish with an ethanol wipe on a Kimwipe. The bowl dries quickly
    from residual heat.
16. After the last sample, clean up, recycle paper, replace the bowl,
    and turn off the shatterbox.


### 7.2 Step 2: Weighing and Mixing

1. Bring your 9 powdered samples to the analytical lab. Get an XRF
   sample sheet from the drawer left of the weigh station and fill out
   the top portion. Place the sheet on a wooden tray (from the cabinet
   in the XRF lab) and keep it next to the balance.
2. Retrieve a small cup of flux from the desiccator (pour from the
   large jug into the cup labeled "Flux").
3. For each sample:
   a. Label a plastic cup lid with the sample number (cross out any
      previous labels). Label the corresponding circle on the XRF
      sample sheet.
   b. Place the cup (no lid) in the cardboard holder on the balance,
      close the sliding door, and zero.
   c. Weigh 3.5000 g ($\pm$ 0.0004 g) of sample powder into the cup.
      Record the exact mass. Zero the balance.
   d. Add 7.0000 g ($\pm$ 0.0004 g) of flux (2:1 flux-to-sample ratio).
      Record the mass. If you add too much flux, remove the excess but
      **do not return it to the reagent container** -- discard it.
   e. If you have less than 3.5 g of sample, weigh what you have and
      adjust the flux to maintain the 2:1 ratio.
   f. Seal the lid tightly.
4. Arrange the cups on the counter in the order they appear on the
   sample sheet.
5. Mix each cup on the Vortex mixer for about one minute, moving the
   cup around on the pad. If powder clings to the sides, pass the
   deionizing bar (red switch) over the cup.


### 7.3 Step 3: First Fusion {#sec-first-fusion}

#### Furnace Startup

1. Flip the black switch on the front of the furnace.
2. Press the T1 temperature button and confirm T = 1000 °C. Adjust on
   the keypad if needed.
3. Set a reasonable duration (e.g., 24, 48, or 72 hours) on the first
   Time/Duration button. If you will use the furnace multiple times in
   a week, set the duration for the full week to reduce thermal cycling
   wear on the heating elements.
4. Press Enter and Start. An audible click confirms the ramp has begun.
   It takes roughly 1 hour to reach 1000 °C.

::: {.callout-caution}
Do not spill glass in the furnace or introduce liquids. Do not use this
furnace for temperatures below 500 °C -- use a regular drying oven
instead. Do not shut off the furnace mid-cycle with the power button;
let it run out its programmed time and shut off automatically.
:::

#### Loading Crucibles

5. Select 9 sturdy-looking graphite crucibles from the drawer under the
   furnace. Clean the inside of each by gently wiping with a Kimwipe
   (avoid scoring the bottom) and blowing out with compressed air under
   the fume hood.
6. Back at the analytical lab, carefully empty each cup into the
   corresponding crucible. Use the deionizing bar if powder clings. Place
   each crucible on its matching circle on the XRF sample sheet.
   **Maintaining the correct order is critical -- once the powder is in
   the crucible, there is no way to tell samples apart.**
7. Place the empty cups (lids on) in the box labeled "Dirty Cups for
   Blowing Out."

#### Fusing

8. In the wet lab, place a tile on the brick stand (small hole facing
   toward you) and crank the stand up until the tile is about halfway up
   the side of the furnace. Arrange the crucibles on the tile in the same
   layout as on the sample sheet (orient so the tile hole corresponds to
   the bottom of the sheet).
9. Put on both long heat-resistant gloves. Using the tongs (drawer under
   the furnace), slide the tile into the furnace. Close the door as
   quickly as possible -- the temperature drops rapidly when the door is
   open.
10. Wait 20--30 minutes for the furnace to recover to 1000 °C, then
    leave the samples for 10--15 minutes. Longer fusion times are
    acceptable and help carbon-rich samples degas fully. Insufficient
    time leads to poor fusions.
11. While fusing, clean the plastic cups: blow out each cup and lid with
    compressed air under the fume hood (do not touch the inside). Discard
    cups that have been used 6 or more times.

#### Removing Crucibles

12. Crank the stand down a few turns. Wearing gloves, open the furnace
    and position the stand in front. Pull the tile out using the tongs
    and the tile hole. Move the stand to the left side and close the
    furnace. Crank the stand down level with the hot plate and slide the
    tile onto it. The hot plate dissipates heat faster than the bricks.

::: {.callout-danger}
The tile and crucibles are extremely hot when removed from the furnace.
Do not touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled.
:::


### 7.4 Step 4: Regrinding and Second Fusion

1. After the crucibles have cooled completely (at least 2 hours), place
   them on the sample sheet in the correct order and take them to the
   rock grinding lab.
2. Set up as before: brown butcher paper, white paper, brush, Brillo
   pad, compressed air, Kimwipes, and ethanol.
3. For each sample, turn the crucible over and gently tap the bead out
   onto the Brillo pad. Scrub off any residual graphite. Place the bead
   in the shatterbox bowl (outside the ring), add a drop of ethanol, and
   grind for 30 seconds.
4. While grinding, clean the crucible (Kimwipe and air).
5. Brush the powder onto a piece of white paper, funnel it back into the
   clean crucible, and return it to the sample sheet. **Do not tamp down
   the powder.** Clean the shatterbox head thoroughly before the next
   sample.
6. Once all 9 samples are reground, take the tray back to the wet lab
   and fuse again as before. The furnace recovers to 1000 °C faster on
   the second round (typically 15--20 minutes). Fuse for 10--15 minutes.

::: {.callout-tip}
This is a good time to prepare sample bags and labels (ask for a
template; bags are in a drawer under the counter in the XRF lab).
:::

7. After removal, check that the glass fully covers the bottom of each
   crucible (look carefully -- do not bring your face close while still
   hot). If the glass is incomplete, wait until the bead is no longer
   glowing orange (a darker red), then gently press the brass rod (drawer
   under the furnace) into the crucible to flatten the glass. Do not
   press so hard that glass flows up around the rod. Repeat if needed.
8. Once the beads have cooled completely, remove them one at a time and
   place each in the correctly labeled bag (following the sample sheet
   order). If any bead is cracked, broken, or has air-bubble holes
   extending more than halfway through, return it to the crucible for a
   third fusion (only a few minutes at 1000 °C are needed).


### 7.5 Step 5: Engraving and Polishing

#### Engraving

1. Take the samples to the darkroom. Turn on the upper light switch.
2. Using the diamond-tipped pen or rotary tool (on the counter at left),
   etch the sample number on the top (non-flat) side of each bead. If
   the top is glassy, either tool works. If carbon is built up on the
   top, use the rotary tool.

#### Polishing

Three important rules for polishing:

- **Keep laps dry when not in use but wet when grinding.** Laps will rust
  if left wet. When finished with a lap, move the water spigot aside and
  spin the wheel at high speed until all water is gone.
- **Do not leave beads in water.** Water will hydrate the glass and
  affect the analysis. If a bead is not actively being polished, dip it
  in ethanol and leave it under the heat lamp to dry.
- **Do not transfer grains between laps.** Rinse the bead in water after
  each stage before moving to the next.

3. Turn on the water to all four laps using the faucet on the right side
   of the sink. Adjust each spigot as needed.
4. Start with the coarse-grain disc (normally far left, ~150 rpm). Place
   the bead flat-side down and slide it across the lap, removing
   irregularities and air bubbles. Generally, at least 1 mm of material
   should be removed from the bottom.
5. Move to the medium lap, removing scratches from the coarse stage.
6. Move to the third (fine) lap, removing scratches from the medium
   stage. Apply moderate pressure at each stage.
7. Rinse the bead in water, dip in ethanol, and leave under the lamp on
   a piece of paper to dry. Repeat for all beads.
8. When finished with a lap, move the spigot aside and spin-dry the lap
   for several minutes.

#### Ultrasonic Cleaning

9. Check the water level in the sonicator and add water if needed.
10. Place 4--5 beads in a beaker, add enough ethanol to cover them, and
    run the sonicator for about 1 minute. **Do not put your hand in the
    sonicator while it is running.**
11. Remove the beads (wearing gloves) and place them on a Kimwipe to dry.


### 7.6 Step 6: Loading and Running the XRF

1. Open the XRF lid and load the dry beads into cups, flat side down.
   Wear gloves and avoid touching the flat (analytical) surface.
2. On the computer, open a "Measure and Analyze" window from the
   SuperQ Manager.
3. Click the multi-cup icon (upper left) to open the Sample Changer.
   Double-click the first cup position (A1). Enter the sample name; set
   type to "Routine," application to "Geology Beads," priority to
   "Normal," and verify that the weights are correct. Click Add. The
   changer advances automatically (A2, A3, etc.). Available positions
   are A1--A8 and B5--B8.
4. Once all samples are entered, click **Measure**.

::: {.callout-note}
If the XRF has not been running recently, the instrument needs to warm up
until the front-panel readouts display 60 and 50. Run the first bead
until those values are reached, then click Abort. Wait for the arm to
return the sample, then click Measure to restart. Running samples before
warm-up can compromise the analysis.
:::

5. The XRF changes samples automatically after each analysis finishes.
   If you have more samples than loaded positions, you can open the lid
   and load additional beads while the instrument runs -- but **do not
   open the lid if the flap is up and the arm is moving**.


### 7.7 Step 7: Retrieving Results

1. Open a "Results Evaluation" window. Set the archive to "Geology
   Beads" and adjust the date range. Use the "Name Mask" field
   (enter your prefix followed by the wildcard character) to filter
   results. Click on a sample and then click "View."
2. To export data: open a "Results Quantitative" window (icon in upper
   left). Adjust date and name mask. Click the Print icon, then
   "Delimited Values Report" to clipboard. Paste into a spreadsheet.


## 8. Quality Control

- Verify the 2:1 flux-to-sample ratio is maintained for every sample.
  Record exact masses on the XRF sample sheet.
- Visually inspect beads before loading: reject cracked, broken, or
  bubble-compromised beads.
- Run laboratory reference standards alongside unknowns to monitor
  instrument drift and accuracy.
- If a bead required a third fusion, note this on the sample sheet.


## 9. Cleanup Checklist

- [ ] All paper recycled (butcher paper, white paper)
- [ ] Shatterbox bowl cleaned and replaced; shatterbox off
- [ ] Chipper cleaned (ethanol wipe on all contact surfaces)
- [ ] Crucibles returned to the drawer (or discarded if degraded)
- [ ] Plastic cups blown out and restocked (or discarded after 6 uses)
- [ ] Polishing laps spun dry
- [ ] Sonicator drained if not in regular use
- [ ] XRF sample sheet completed and filed
- [ ] All personal items removed from the lab
- [ ] Work surfaces wiped down


## 10. Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                   | Possible Cause / Action                          |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| Glass does not cover crucible bottom       | Insufficient fusion time; re-fuse longer         |
| Bead cracked or has deep air bubbles       | Air trapped during fusion; re-fuse briefly       |
| Carbon pellet at bottom of bead            | Carbon not fully degassed; fuse longer next time |
| Powder clings to plastic cup walls         | Pass the deionizing bar over the cup             |
| Shatterbox head has stuck-on powder        | Run sand for 15 seconds; scrub with Brillo pad   |
| XRF front-panel numbers not at 60/50       | Instrument not warmed up; run a bead until ready |
| XRF data appear anomalous                  | Sample may have been run before warm-up; re-run  |

For problems you cannot resolve, contact the lab technician, Jade Star,
or Bob.


## 11. Definitions

- **Fusion bead:** A glass disc produced by melting a mixture of powdered
  rock sample and lithium tetraborate flux at 1000 °C. The homogeneous
  glass eliminates mineralogical effects during XRF analysis.
- **Flux:** Dilithium tetraborate (Li~2~B~4~O~7~), a reagent that lowers
  the melting point of the sample and produces a homogeneous glass.
- **Shatterbox:** A vibratory ring-and-puck mill used to grind rock chips
  to a fine powder.
- **SuperQ:** The PANalytical software used to control the XRF
  spectrometer, define measurement sequences, and retrieve results.
- **Geology Beads:** The SuperQ application/archive configured for
  major-element oxide analysis of fusion beads.
